title: GraphRAG methods to create optimized LLM context windows for Retrieval — Jonathan Larson, Microsoft

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The core subject is GraphRAG, a graph-based RAG architecture for retrieving and grounding knowledge in LLM context windows. GraphRAG is a general retrieval method applied to code repositories (coding_assistants) and scientific co-reasoning (scientific_research), with knowledge retrieval as the foundation (search_and_knowledge). The talk spans research on GraphRAG methods, release of an open-source evaluation benchmark, and announced production deployment in Azure Local and Microsoft Discovery. Assumes familiarity with RAG, embeddings, and graph concepts but is presented for a practitioner conference audience. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair with live demonstrations and quantitative benchmark results. Claims are supported by live code demos, quantitative benchmarks against vector RAG, and an open-source evaluation framework.

summary: Jonathan Larson leads the graph team at Microsoft Research and presents GraphRAG methods for creating optimized LLM context windows. He opens by referencing last year's influential GraphRAG paper and GitHub repository, noting it inspired many derivative offerings. He states two key takeaways: structured LLM memory is essential for effective AI applications, and agents paired with graph structures unlock even greater power. The talk has three parts. First, Larson demonstrates GraphRAG applied to code. A 200-line, 7-file terminal game is used as a test case. Regular RAG produces a useless generic answer, while GraphRAG delivers deep semantic understanding including game mechanics and controls. He shows Python-to-Rust code translation: direct LLM translation fails to compile, but GraphRAG's translation works out of the box. Scaling to the Doom codebase (~100,000 lines, 231 files), GraphRAG enables repository-level documentation via global queries and local queries. A standout demo uses GitHub Copilot's coding agent wired to GraphRAG to add jump capability to Doom, requiring multi-file modification that previously failed with other agents but worked successfully. Second, Larson announces Benchmark QED, now open source on GitHub, for measuring and evaluating GraphRAG-style systems. It has three components: AutoQ for query generation across local/global and data-driven/activity-driven dimensions, AutoE for evaluation using LLM-as-judge with metrics including comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and relevance, and AutoD for dataset summarization and sampling. Third, he presents Lazy GraphRAG benchmark results comparing it to vector RAG on 8K, 120K, and 1M token context windows. Lazy GraphRAG wins 92%, 90%, and 91% of the time against vector RAG on data-local questions, dominating across both local and global question types—a surprising result since RAG was expected to perform better on local questions. Long context windows made little difference, and Lazy GraphRAG cost a tenth of the 1M token context window approach. Larson concludes by announcing Lazy GraphRAG will be incorporated into Azure Local and the Microsoft Discovery platform, which does graph-based scientific co-reasoning.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Talk Overview
sections.summary: Jonathan Larson introduces himself as leader of the graph team at Microsoft Research, references last year's GraphRAG paper and GitHub repo. He outlines two key themes: structured LLM memory as essential for AI applications, and agents paired with graph structures as more powerful. He previews three talk segments: graph for code, Benchmark QED open-source release, and Lazy GraphRAG benchmark results.

sections.title: GraphRAG for Code: Terminal Game Demo
sections.summary: Larson demonstrates GraphRAG for Code on a 200-line, 7-file terminal game. Regular RAG gives a useless generic answer; GraphRAG provides semantic understanding of game mechanics, controls, and architecture. He explains the local vs global query distinction, with this being a global query requiring whole-repository understanding.

sections.title: Code Translation: Python to Rust
sections.summary: Larson shows Python-to-Rust translation of the terminal game. Direct LLM translation generates Rust code but it fails to compile. GraphRAG for Code's translate function generates Rust files that work out of the box, demonstrating the value of graph structure for code translation.

sections.title: Doom Codebase: Documentation and Feature Development
sections.summary: Scaling to the Doom codebase (~100K lines, 231 files), Larson shows GraphRAG generating repository-level documentation via global queries (module-level understanding like the sound system) and local queries (individual files). He then demonstrates adding jump capability to Doom using GitHub Copilot coding agent wired to GraphRAG for Code, successfully performing multi-file modification that other agents failed at.

sections.title: Benchmark QED Announcement and Components
sections.summary: Larson announces Benchmark QED, now open source on GitHub, for measuring and evaluating GraphRAG-style systems on local and global quality metrics. He introduces AutoQ as the first component, focused on query generation for target datasets.

sections.title: Benchmark QED Components Detail and AutoQ Examples
sections.summary: Larson details the three Benchmark QED components: AutoQ (query generation), AutoE (LLM-as-judge evaluation), and AutoD (dataset summarization and sampling). AutoQ generates questions across local/global and data-driven/activity-driven dimensions. He shows sample questions from an AP news medical dataset, contrasting a data-local question (junior doctors striking in South Korea) with an activity-global question (public health initiatives for underserved communities) that requires holistic dataset understanding.

sections.title: Lazy GraphRAG Benchmark Results
sections.summary: Larson presents Lazy GraphRAG benchmark results using AutoE metrics (comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, relevance). Lazy GraphRAG is compared to vector RAG on 8K, 120K, and 1M token context windows. It wins 92%, 90%, and 91% of the time on data-local questions, surprisingly dominating across both local and global question types. Long context windows made little difference, and Lazy GraphRAG cost a tenth of the 1M token approach.

sections.title: Lazy GraphRAG Product Launches and Conclusion
sections.summary: Larson announces Lazy GraphRAG will be incorporated into Azure Local and the Microsoft Discovery platform, which does graph-based scientific co-reasoning (hypothesis, experiment, learning, knowledge) powered by GraphRAG and Lazy GraphRAG. He concludes with final takeaways: structured LLM memory is a powerful tool, and agents can massively amplify this power.
